study.title: Psalm 125 Trust in the protection of the Lord and destiny of the wicked
study.overview: This psalm expresses the security of God's people in the midst of pressure and instability. The first two verses use images of firmness and protection to claim that those who trust the Lord remain unshakable and surrounded by his guard. Then the text shows that the dominion of wickedness will not remain forever on the righteous, because God will not allow corruption to lead them permanently to perversity. The psalm ends with a prayer asking for good for the good and with a serious statement: those who deviate to tortuous ways will be removed with the practitioners of wickedness, while peace is pronounced upon Israel.

outline.title: Confidence Stays and Protection Around
outline.explanation: Those who trust in the Lord are likened to mount Zion: firm, stable and not easily shaken. The image of the mountains around Jerusalem reinforces that the Lord surrounds his people with lasting protection.

outline.title: Limit to the domination of wickedness
outline.explanation: The psalm states that the scepter of perversity will not remain on the righteous forever. The preservation of God includes preventing the pressure of evil from leading the righteous to surrender to injustice.

outline.title: Prayer for the righteous and judgment on the deviated
outline.explanation: The psalmist asks the Lord to do good to those who are good and upright in heart. At the same time, he declares that those who follow tortuous ways will be turned away with the wicked, and end with a blessing of peace upon Israel.

study.context: The notes provided suggest a community reading of the psalm, linked to the trust of God's people in their protection and to prayer for peace. Adam Clarke understands that the psalm probably belongs to the period after captivity and associates it interpretively with the resistances faced by the Jews by rebuilding Jerusalem. As this comes from a commentator, it should be read as a proposal of context, not as a certainty imposed by the text.
study.theology: The psalm unites security, holiness and judgment. First, trust in the Lord is not mere religious emotion, but a foundation of spiritual stability. Second, divine protection does not mean absence of conflict, but a presence surrounding God in the midst of external and internal pressures. Third, the text shows that God's faithfulness includes sustaining the righteous and also limiting the influence of wickedness, so that the covenant is not corrupted. Finally, prayer for good to the good and the exclusion of those who deviate show that biblical peace is not indifferent to sin: it is born from God's righteous action for his people.

scholarViews.insight: The commentator points out that the psalm expresses community confidence in the protection of the Lord and concludes with a prayer for peace.
He observes that those who trust in the Lord and are righteous receive the promises of God: be established, kept and not always under oppression.
The commentator links the image of Jerusalem's encircling to God's providential protection, as a defense surrounding his people.

questions: In which areas of my life do I need to rely more on the stability that comes from the Lord, and not on circumstances?
Does my way of life show righteousness of heart or some tortuous path that needs to be abandoned?
How can I pray and act to promote the peace of God's people without relativizing holiness?
study.practice: This week, choose a situation in which you feel pressured to give in. Pray on the basis of the psalm asking the Lord to encircle him with his protection and give him firmness to stand on the right path. I also intercede with other believers who are under pressure, asking God to do them well and strengthen their hearts. If there is any habit or tortuous decision in your life, name it before God and take a concrete step of repentance and correction.
study.uncertainty: The text does not inform authorship or date, and any specific historical association, such as the reconstruction of Jerusalem after captivity, comes only from a commentary interpretation. The images of Zion, Jerusalem and mountains are poetic; therefore, the details should not be transformed into an exact geographical description. Notes also allow different devotional readings about who are the righteous and those who deviate, so that the application must remain subordinate to the sense of psalm and not to a specific denominational tradition.
